- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. - codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan or design. Use when the user wants to stress-test a plan before building, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- research: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a Markdown file in the repo. Use when the user wants a topic researched, docs or API facts gathered, or reading legwork delegated to a background agent.
- seo-optimizer: Optimize content for search engines with keyword analysis, readability scoring, meta descriptions, and competitor comparison. Use this when users want to improve SEO, optimize blog posts, or analyze content for search performance.
- systems-thinking: Analyze problems using a Systems Thinking approach. Use when users mention "systems thinking," "systemic," "feedback loops," "unintended consequences," "root cause," "interconnected," or request analysis of complex, multi-factor problems. Guides conversation through questions and observations rather than prescriptive solutions.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- copilot-fetch-x: Fetch the content of an X (Twitter) post using Copilot Plus. Use when the user shares an x.com or twitter.com URL and wants its text or context. Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- copilot-read-pdf: Extract the full text of a PDF as Markdown using Copilot Plus. Use when the user wants to read, summarize, or quote a PDF file (in the vault or an absolute path). Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- copilot-web-fetch: Fetch and read the full contents of a specific web page (URL) as clean Markdown using Copilot Plus. Use when the user shares a link or asks you to open, read, or summarize a particular page — not for an open-ended web search. Requires an active Copilot Plus license; without it, use your own fetch tool instead.
- copilot-web-search: Search the web for current information using Copilot Plus. Use when the user asks to search online, look something up on the internet, or needs up-to-date facts beyond the vault. Prefer reading the vault for anything about the user's own notes. Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- copilot-youtube-transcript: Fetch the transcript of a YouTube video using Copilot Plus. Use when the user shares a YouTube URL and wants its contents, a summary, or quotes. Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- miyo-search: Semantic (meaning-based) search over the user's Obsidian vault via the local Miyo app. For any vault-search intent, use it when builtin grep search is too slow or doesn't surface enough relevant notes, or when the user explicitly asks for Miyo search. Needs the Miyo desktop app installed and running.
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

73	**Purpose:** A quarterly check-in workflow that reviews the calendar quarter Mark is closing out (calendar, email volume, completed work), rolls up quarter-level analytics and marketing experiments, surfaces a few Content Ideas, scans what's ahead, and produces a summary with priorities. ## Routine Skills

### Quarterly Review
**Purpose:** A quarterly check-in workflow that reviews the calendar quarter Mark is closing out (calendar, email volume, completed work), rolls up quarter-level analytics and marketing experiments, surfaces a few Content Ideas, scans what's ahead, and produces a summary with priorities. Includes a read-only git work-recap across the APR repos (agile-pain-relief-astro, social-media-posting) summarizing what shipped, grouped by theme. The weekly review scaled to a quarter, but **read-only** - it deliberately omits the OmniFocus inbox sweep and the Drafts cleanup. In-chat only; never saved to a file; no reflective questions. LifeHQ-Mark is excluded by a global deny rule. Window defaults to the quarter being closed out (mid-quarter → quarter start through today; early in a new quarter → the full just-ended quarter).

Includes a read-only git work-recap across the APR repos (agile-pain-relief-astro, social-media-posting) summarizing what shipped, grouped by theme. In-chat only -- never saved to a file; no reflective questions. LifeHQ-Mark is excluded by a global deny rule.
**Triggers:** "weekly review", "how'd my week go", "plan my week", "Sunday review", "what did I ship this week", "weekly work summary", "recap the repos"

Roles map to folders; Arete statements live in Self/Roles.md.

## APR Skills

### Blog Critique
**Purpose:** Critiques a draft blog post against Mark's established writing style. Flags tone slips, off-voice vocabulary, and clunky sentence structures, plus a logic and content gap analysis and a dependency-order (information-DAG) check that section order grounds each term/concept before a later section leans on it. No rewrites. When the draft is a Markdown file, delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup (see criticmarkup-editing); chat bullets are the fallback for pasted text.
**Triggers:** "critique this blog post", "review my blog draft", "blog critique", "voice check my blog", "does this blog sound like me"
**File:** `Skills/APR/blog-critique/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format)

### Competitive Landscape
**Purpose:** Competitive analysis frameworks (Porter's Five Forces, Blue Ocean, positioning maps) tailored for APR's Scrum/Agile training and GenAI-for-business-agility market. Writes new analyses to `APR/Analytics/`.
**Triggers:** "analyze competitors", "competitive landscape", "identify differentiation", "market positioning", "Porter's Five Forces"
**File:** `Skills/APR/competitive-landscape/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Existing APR competitive docs in `APR/Analytics/` (e.g. `genai-course-competitive-analysis.md`)

### Content Performance
**Purpose:** Analyze APR content performance across social media, email newsletters, and website traffic. Reads raw data from the Astro repo (`agile-pain-relief-astro/analytics/`), writes a single live snapshot to `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md` (overwrite, not dated).
**Triggers:** "content performance", "analyze my content", "how are my posts doing", "newsletter engagement", "which topics perform best", "social to website traffic"
**File:** `Skills/APR/content-performance/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Bash access to Astro repo analytics folder, `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` for matching newsletter content

### Linkedin Style
**Purpose:** Two modes for Mark's LinkedIn presence. Review mode (default) critiques draft posts against Mark's voice and LinkedIn-specific conventions (length, hooks, emoji, hashtags, external links) and delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup on a Markdown file (chat is the fallback for pasted text). Draft mode generates 2-3 complete draft-post options from a topic Mark gives or from his blog/glossary/newsletter content, built mostly by reusing his own sentences and phrasing from the source so the draft already sounds like him and he can edit rather than start blank. Covers Scrum/Agile posts, GenAI/LLM posts (skeptical-pragmatist lean), personal posts, and business announcements.
**Triggers:** "review this LinkedIn post", "critique my post", "LinkedIn style", "LinkedIn rubric", "post review", "does this post sound like me", "voice check on this post", "draft a LinkedIn post", "give me LinkedIn post ideas", "draft LinkedIn options", "LinkedIn post from this newsletter", "draft some posts on"
**File:** `Skills/APR/linkedin-style/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format); reference newsletters in `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` optional for calibration; cross-platform emoji policy in `_social-posting-conventions.md` (agile-pain-relief-astro repo)

### Newsletter Reading Recap
**Purpose:** Builds the "Mark's Reading Rabbit Hole" section for the newsletter — a paste-ready Markdown list of what Mark read since the last issue, linked to originals, with neutral one-line descriptions. Papers and PDFs lead; archived-without-highlights items are demoted to a short trailing list. Window defaults to "since the last newsletter" (auto-detected from the Newsletter folder). Skips any article already featured in the reading section of the last 15 issues (exclusion set derived from the newsletter files themselves, reading-section links only, URL-normalized); the window can widen further back since repeats are filtered. Read-only and print-to-chat only; never edits the newsletter file.
**Triggers:** "reading recap for the newsletter", "reading rabbit hole", "what should go in the newsletter reading list", "newsletter reading section"
**File:** `Skills/APR/newsletter-reading-recap/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Readwise CLI (preferred) or Readwise MCP; reads `Skills/Readwise/readwise-cli/SKILL.md` for command reference

### Newsletter Reviewer
**Purpose:** Reviews and critiques draft newsletters against Mark's authentic voice, tone, and style guidelines. Produces a structured critique with anti-pattern detections, terminology checks, a provisional subject-line check (filename-derived line plus any `// Subject A:` / `// Subject B:` A/B variants), and priority fixes. When the draft is a Markdown file, delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup (see criticmarkup-editing); chat critique is the fallback for pasted text.
**Triggers:** "review my newsletter", "critique this draft", "does this sound like me", "voice check", "newsletter rubric", "style check", "review my subject line", "subject line check"
**File:** `Skills/APR/newsletter-reviewer/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format)

### Reshare Queue Tune
**Purpose:** Quarterly performance re-tier of the social-media reshare queue in `complete-social-media-calendar.md`. Measures how each already-posted queue item performed when reshared (PostHog `archive-reshare` attribution, LinkedIn-weighted, normalised to clicks-per-reshare) plus social engagement from `history.json`, then proposes tier moves (promote to TIER 2 / demote / retire) and surfaces high-traffic pages not yet queued. This is the **major** update; the monthly **minor** update (curate newly published posts/glossary via `calendar-audit`) does not need this skill. Approval gate before editing; refreshes the header with `calendar-audit --write`.
**Triggers:** "tune the reshare queue", "re-tier the calendar", "which reshares are working", "reshare queue review", "quarterly social queue update"
**File:** `Skills/APR/reshare-queue-tune/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `apr-weekly-analytics` (data refresh), `apr-content-performance` (optional context), `calendar-audit` in the `social-media-posting` repo, Bash access to Astro repo analytics; pairs with `quarterly-review`

### Seo Audit
**Purpose:** Diagnose structural SEO issues on agilepainrelief.com. Five-section audit framework (Crawlability, Technical, On-Page, Content/E-E-A-T, Authority) tightened for an Astro content/blog site. Produces a prioritised findings report at `APR/Analytics/seo-audit-YYYY-MM-DD.md`. Findings only, no auto-fix.

**File:** `Skills/APR/seo-audit/SKILL.md`

### Weekly Analytics
**Purpose:** Orchestrate the weekly analytics loop — run `npm run scrape` and `npm run posthog-export` in the Astro repo, invoke `apr-content-performance` to regenerate the live report, flag experiment follow-ups, capture tasks to OmniFocus.
**Triggers:** "run weekly analytics", "refresh analytics", "pull analytics", "weekly data pull"
**File:** `Skills/APR/weekly-analytics/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `apr-content-performance`, `omnifocus-capture`, `omnifocus-workflow`, Bash access to Astro repo

---

## Writing Skills

### Criticmarkup Editing
**Purpose:** Default delivery format for feedback on Mark's Markdown writing -- annotate the file in place with CriticMarkup (comments `{>>Claude: …<<}`, additions `{++…++}`, deletions `{--…--}`, substitutions `{~~old~>new~~}`, highlights `{==…==}`), reviewed in Obsidian's Track Changes side panel. The voice rubrics decide WHAT to flag; this skill decides HOW to deliver it. Always delivers the full markup pass in one go (no section-by-section chunking; the CLAUDE.md chunked-review preference does not apply to CriticMarkup passes). Applies to all writing types including sales/marketing copy. Never rewrites Mark's prose outside a markup wrapper. Falls back to chat bullets for pasted (non-file) content.
**Triggers:** "edit this", "mark up my draft", "track changes", "use CriticMarkup", "suggest edits inline", "give me feedback on my writing"
**File:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Obsidian Track Changes plugin (`.obsidian/plugins/track-changes/`); read alongside the relevant voice rubric (apr-blog-critique, apr-newsletter-reviewer, apr-linkedin-style, Marketing/copy-editing, storybrand-messaging)

### Email Voice
**Purpose:** Mark's email writing voice, for a dictation tool to draft emails that sound like him. Covers shared structure, professional vs personal registers, mechanics, and a dictation correction/vocabulary list. Built from analysis of 50+ sent emails.
**Triggers:** "draft an email", "write this email in my voice", "email in my voice", "make this email sound like me", "reply to this email as me"
**File:** `Skills/Writing/email-voice/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** None

## Communication Skills

### Drafts Inbox
**Purpose:** Triages everything in the Drafts inbox (no longer keyed to a "cowork" tag), classifies each item, takes action, and archives when done so the inbox stays the unprocessed queue. For a large backlog, asks how far back to go and filters by `modificationDate`. Tasks route to `omnifocus-capture`.
**Triggers:** "check my Drafts inbox", "process my inbox", "what's in Drafts", "triage my Drafts inbox", "drafts inbox triage"
**File:** `Skills/Comms/drafts-inbox/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Drafts MCP connector; `Skills/OmniFocus/capture/SKILL.md` (for task capture)

### Gmail Triage
**Purpose:** Recommend a triage plan for the Gmail inbox via the Gmail MCP. Classifies each thread into one of four actions — reference (file under existing label), reply-needed (draft suggestion only), trash, or archive (remove INBOX, keep in All Mail for records) — with a Task overlay for emails that imply an OmniFocus action. All recommendations require explicit per-item approval, presented in batches of 10. Replies handled in a separate pass. Only uses existing labels; never creates new ones. Trashing uses the Gmail TRASH label (30-day recovery). Sender-specific rules and aging rules live in `memory/feedback_gmail_triage.md`. Task captures delegate to `omnifocus-capture`.
**Triggers:** "triage my Gmail", "process my Gmail inbox", "Gmail triage", "sort my Gmail", "Gmail inbox zero"
**File:** `Skills/Comms/gmail-triage/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Gmail MCP connector (authenticated), `Skills/OmniFocus/capture/SKILL.md` (for Task overlay), `memory/feedback_gmail_triage.md` (sender rules)

### Growthmaterial Export
**Purpose:** Export emails labelled `Courses and Memberships/GrowthMaterial` to Markdown under `~/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/3 - YFL/14 - TRAININGS & BIZ DEV/GrowthInReverse/Emails/`. Resumable across sessions via `_processed.json` state. Strips newsletter chrome (footer, tracking pixels, layout tables), downloads inline images locally to `images/`, names files `YYYY-MM-DD-sender-subject-slug.md` with YAML frontmatter. Skips Mark's own SENT forwards inside threads and the mis-labelled Scrum forum thread. Heavy lifting done by `_export.py` next to the output folder; Claude orchestrates one thread at a time to manage context burn from inline MCP returns. Optional duplicate detection pass at the end compares each new file against the sibling course-content folders (Growth/Monetization/Retention/Subscriber-Onboarding) and presents candidates for approval before deletion.
**Triggers:** "export GrowthMaterial emails", "update GrowthInReverse emails", "fetch new growth emails", "sync GrowthMaterial folder"
**File:** `Skills/Comms/growthmaterial-export/SKILL.md`

# APR Weekly Analytics Loop

Runs the end-to-end weekly analytics refresh: pull fresh data into the Astro repo, run the analyzer skill, save the live report, flag follow-ups.

## When to Use

- Mark's weekly review cadence (paired with `weekly-review`)
- Any time Mark wants current content performance data
- Before a newsletter planning session or marketing decision

## Paths

- **Astro repo (for pull scripts):** `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro`
- **Live report output:** `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md` (overwrite, do not date-stamp)

Raw-data paths and the full data dictionary live in `apr-content-performance`; that skill owns them. This loop just pulls fresh data, invokes the analyzer, and handles follow-ups.

## Steps

### 1. Pull fresh raw data

Run these in the Astro repo (ask Mark to confirm before running, since these hit external APIs / scrapers):

```bash
cd /Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro
npm run scrape
npm run posthog-export
npm run scrape-engagement
```

- `npm run scrape` pulls social media engagement from Buffer via Playwright into `analytics/history.json`
- `npm run posthog-export` pulls PostHog pageviews / sessions / bounce rate into `analytics/posthog/`
- `npm run scrape-engagement` pulls newsletter engagement from Cakemail into `analytics/email-engagement/newsletter-engagement.json` (merges with and preserves the old Drip history)

**Freshness checks (manual data sources):**

Before running the analyzer, stat these files and compare against the thresholds below. If any are stale, surface to Mark and offer the matching refresh path.

| Source | Path | Threshold | Refresh path |
|---|---|---|---|
| Google Search Console | `analytics/google/` (latest entry) | 30 days | Manual monthly export. Use the `Google Search Console Export` task in the APR `Operations` project: surface the export page and let Mark do it. Do NOT automate or scrape it. Export page: `https://search.google.com/search-console/performance/search-analytics?resource_id=sc-domain%3Aagilepainrelief.com&hl=en-GB`. Save under `analytics/google/agilepainrelief.com-Performance-on-Search-YYYY-MM-DD`. |
| Ahrefs | `analytics/Ahrefs/` (latest entry) | 30 days | Subscription ended — note as permanently stale, don't prompt |

Check pattern (Bash):

```bash
ls -lt /Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro/analytics/google/ | head -2
```

Compute age in days. If stale, report to Mark with the recommended refresh action before moving to step 2.

### 2. Invoke the analyzer

Run `apr-content-performance` to regenerate the live report. The analyzer reads from the Astro paths and writes to `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md`.

Ask Mark what lens he wants for this week's report, or default to a standard rollup:

- Top 10 posts by social engagement (past 4 weeks)
- Top 10 newsletter CTR / unsub rate (past 8 issues)
- Top 10 pages by traffic, grouped by UTM source
- Notable changes vs. the prior report (if a prior snapshot is available)

### 3. Scan for experiment signals

Read `APR/Analytics/Experiments/_Experiments Index.md`. For each **active** experiment:

- Check whether the latest data supports updating **Result** or **Learning** fields
- Flag experiments where measurement is overdue (e.g. Internal Linking strategy was due for a June 2026 check)
- Each experiment is tracked in two linked places: the vault note here and a task in the `Marketing Experiments` OF project. A follow-up usually means touching both.
- Do NOT write to the experiment notes without Mark's approval; surface findings for him to review

### 4. Capture follow-ups to OmniFocus

If the report surfaces tasks, use `omnifocus-capture` to record them. Route by mode (see `omnifocus-workflow.md`):

- **One-off tasks** (e.g. "consolidate /choose-the-right-scrum-course and /course-selector pages", "respond to comment thread on LinkedIn post X") → inbox; Mark triages.
- **Experiment follow-up** (data supports updating an experiment, or one needs a next action) → the matching task in the `Marketing Experiments` project: flag it for the week or update its note, and update the experiment's vault note in `APR/Analytics/Experiments/`. Don't create a project per experiment; the structure is one task per experiment.
- **Recurring monitoring** (a check that should repeat on a cadence) → a task in `Operations`.

### 5. Brief Mark

Output a short summary in chat (not saved to a file):

- What changed this week (top 3-5 signals)
- Experiment status updates worth his attention
- Tasks captured to OmniFocus (if any)
- Anything stale or missing (e.g. "Ahrefs data is 6 weeks old, consider refreshing")

## Safety Rails

- **Confirm before running `npm` scripts.** They're network-hitting and moderately slow. Show Mark the commands first.
- **Never modify raw data files.** `history.json`, CSVs, and JSON exports are write-only by the pull scripts. Analysis reads them.
- **Overwrite `content-performance-snapshot.md`, don't version it.** Mark wants one place to look for current data.
- **Experiment notes are Mark-edited.** Flag updates; do not write to `APR/Analytics/Experiments/*.md` without approval.

## Dependencies

- `apr-content-performance` (does the actual analysis)
- `omnifocus-capture` (for follow-up tasks)
- `omnifocus-workflow` (for capture conventions)
- Bash access to the Astro repo

## Related

- `weekly-review` — the broader weekly review; analytics-pull is one step in that rhythm
- `apr-newsletter-reviewer` — for newsletter draft reviews (not part of this loop)

## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

1	---
2	name: "content-performance"
3	category: "APR"
4	triggered: true
5	triggers: ["content performance", "analyze my content", "how are my posts doing", "newsletter engagement", "which topics perform best", "social to website traffic"]
6	purpose: "Analyze APR content performance across social media, email newsletters, and website traffic. Reads raw data from the Astro repo (`agile-pain-relief-astro/analytics/`), writes a single live snapshot to `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md` (overwrite, not dated)."
7	dependencies: ["Bash access to Astro repo analytics folder, `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` for matching newsletter content"]
8	description: Analyze APR content performance across social media, email newsletters, and website traffic. Use when asked to evaluate content performance, compare platforms, identify top-performing topics, correlate social/email engagement with website traffic, or analyze newsletter engagement patterns.
9	triggers:
10	  - content performance
11	  - analyze my content
12	  - how are my posts doing
13	  - newsletter engagement
14	  - which topics perform best
15	  - social to website traffic
16	---
17	
18	# APR Content Performance Analyzer
19	
20	Analyze how APR content performs across three channels: social media (LinkedIn, Mastodon, Bluesky), email newsletters (Drip), and website traffic (PostHog).
21	
22	**Raw data lives in the Astro repo** (because the pull scripts write there). Analysis and findings live in the vault. This skill reads from the Astro paths below and writes output to the vault's APR/Analytics folder.
23	
24	## Paths
25	
26	**Raw data (read-only from Astro repo):**
27	
28	- Social engagement: `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro/analytics/history.json`
29	- Newsletter engagement: `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro/analytics/email-engagement/newsletter-engagement.json`
30	- PostHog exports: `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro/analytics/posthog/*.csv`
31	- Ahrefs exports: `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro/analytics/Ahrefs/`
32	- Google Search Console exports: `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro/analytics/google/`
33	
34	**Analysis outputs (vault):**
35	
36	- Single live report (overwrite, don't date): `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md`
37	- Newsletter findings reference: `APR/Analytics/email-engagement-findings.md`
38	- Newsletter content (for matching engagement to text): `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/*.md`
39	- Experiments tracking: `APR/Analytics/Experiments/`
40	
41	**Writing one live report, not dated snapshots, is intentional** — Mark wants one place to look for current data. History is not important.
42	
43	## Data Sources
44	
45	### Post Engagement — `history.json`
46	
47	Array of post objects. Each post has:
48	
49	| Field | Type | Description |
50	|-------|------|-------------|
51	| `id` | number | Unique post identifier |
52	| `created` | string | Date post was created (YYYY-MM-DD) |
53	| `posted` | string | Date post was published (YYYY-MM-DD), empty if unposted |
54	| `linkedin` | string | LinkedIn post text |
55	| `mastodon` | array/string | Mastodon thread parts |
56	| `bluesky` | string | Bluesky thread text |
57	| `topics` | array | Topic tags (e.g. `["scrum", "agile"]`) |
58	| `links` | array | URLs included in the post |
59	| `engagement` | object | Per-platform engagement metrics (see below) |
60	
61	#### Engagement metrics by platform
62	
63	- **LinkedIn**: `reactions`, `comments`, `impressions`, `reach`, `engagementRate`
64	- **Mastodon**: `favorites`, `replies`, `reblogs`
65	- **Bluesky**: `likes`, `comments`, `reposts`
66	
67	Not all posts have engagement on all platforms. Some posts have no engagement data at all.
68	
69	### Email Newsletter Engagement — `newsletter-engagement.json`
70	
71	Object with `lastUpdated` timestamp and `newsletters` array. Each newsletter has:
72	
73	| Field | Type | Description |
74	|-------|------|-------------|
75	| `id` | string | Drip email identifier |
76	| `name` | string | Internal newsletter name |
77	| `subject` | string | Email subject line |
78	| `sendDate` | string | Date sent (YYYY-MM-DD), empty if unsent |
79	| `opens` | number | Email open count |
80	| `clicks` | number | Total link clicks |
81	| `unsubscribes` | number | Unsubscribe count from this email |
82	| `linkClicks` | array | Per-link click breakdown (recent newsletters only) |
83	
84	Each item in `linkClicks` has: `url`, `text` (link label), `clicks` (count). Detail available from ~Aug 2025 onward.
85	
86	#### Key metrics
87	
88	- **Click-through rate (CTR)**: `clicks / opens * 100` — average is ~5.5%
89	- **Unsubscribe rate**: `unsubscribes / opens * 100` — average is ~0.66%
90	- **Link click categories**: blog_post, glossary_entry, course_page, external_resource, social_media, homepage, lead_magnet, webinar, lean_coffee, survey, waitlist_signup
91	
92	#### Newsletter content source files
93	
94	Full newsletter content (with all links, sections, and body text) is in Obsidian at `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/*.md`. Each file has YAML frontmatter with `id`, `subject`, `name`, `from_name`, `from_email`, `status`, `send_at`, and `created_at`. Match engagement records to content via the `id` field or by date/subject.
95	
96	#### Established findings
97	
98	Read `APR/Analytics/email-engagement-findings.md` for the durable findings:
99	
100	- **Best-performing topic**: Meetings/facilitation (12.6% CTR, 0.18% unsub rate)
101	- **Strongest content format**: Long-form articles embedded in the email body
102	- **AI/GenAI topics**: Above-average CTR (6.57%), below-average unsub rate (0.59%)
103	- **Weakest performers**: Generic Scrum practice topics (3.18% CTR), abstract theory, pure announcements
104	- **Blog post clicks dominate**: 21.4% of all link clicks
105	- **Glossary entry clicks are minimal**: Only 1.3%
106	- **Mastodon profile link**: Surprisingly popular (167 clicks across 13 newsletters)
107	- **Opens declining**: 22% drop from 2023 peak to early 2026
108	
109	### Website Traffic — PostHog CSVs
110	
111	Three CSV files with date-stamped filenames (e.g. `*-2026-02-09.csv`). Use glob patterns to find the latest files.
112	
113	#### Pageviews by week, UTM source, and pathname
114	- **File pattern**: `export-pageviews-by-week-utm-source-and-pathname-*.csv`
115	- **Columns**: `week`, `utm_source`, `pathname`, `daily_active_users`
116	- **UTM sources**: `mastodon`, `linkedin`, `drip` (email), `website`, `blog`, `chatgpt.com`, `None` (direct/organic)
117	
118	#### Average session duration by UTM source by week
119	- **File pattern**: `export-average-sessions-by-utm-source-by-week-*.csv`
120	- **Columns**: `week`, `utm_source`, `total_sessions`, `avg_session_duration_seconds`, `avg_session_duration_minutes`
121	
122	#### Bounce rate by UTM source and pathname
123	- **File pattern**: `export-bounce-rate-percentage-by-week-*.csv`
124	- **Columns**: `utm_source`, `pathname`, `bounced_sessions`, `total_sessions`, `bounce_rate_pct`
125	
126	## Analysis Types
127	
128	### 1. Cross-Platform Engagement Comparison
129	
130	Compare how the same post performs across LinkedIn, Mastodon, and Bluesky.
131	
132	**Method:** Read `history.json`, filter to posts with engagement on 2+ platforms, normalize metrics, identify platform-specific winners.
133	
134	### 2. Social → Website Traffic Correlation
135	
136	Connect social posts to website traffic by matching post links to PostHog pathnames.
137	
138	**Method:** Read `history.json`, extract `links`, convert to pathnames. Read pageviews CSV, filter by `utm_source = mastodon` or `linkedin`. Match dates to weekly pageview data.
139	
140	### 3. Topic Performance Analysis
141	
142	Identify which topics generate the most engagement and traffic.
143	
144	**Method:** Group `history.json` posts by `topics`, aggregate engagement across platforms, cross-reference PostHog pageviews for linked pages.
145	
146	### 4. Traffic Source Quality
147	
148	Compare how traffic from different social platforms behaves on the website.
149	
150	**Method:** Compare session duration, bounce rate, and total visitors by UTM source across the three PostHog CSVs.
151	
152	### 5. Content-to-Traffic Pipeline
153	
154	End-to-end view: which posts drove the most qualified website traffic?
155	
156	**Method:** Combine posts with links to agilepainrelief.com → PostHog traffic by path and UTM source → session duration → bounce rate. Rank by downstream website impact.
157	
158	### 6. Posting Cadence Analysis
159	
160	Group `history.json` posts by week/month using `posted` dates, calculate average engagement per period, compare high- vs. low-frequency weeks.
161	
162	### 7. Newsletter Engagement Analysis
163	
164	**Method:**
165	1. Filter `newsletter-engagement.json` to newsletters with opens > 100
166	2. Calculate CTR and unsub rate per newsletter
167	3. Categorize by topic from subject lines (AI/GenAI, Scrum Practices, Team/People, Meetings, Engineering/Quality, Metrics/Flow, Leadership, etc.)
168	4. Aggregate metrics per topic
169	5. For newsletters with `linkClicks` data, categorize each link and aggregate clicks by category
170	
171	**Link categorization rules:**
172	- `agilepainrelief.com/blog/` → blog_post
173	- `agilepainrelief.com/glossary/` → glossary_entry
174	- `agilepainrelief.com/(certified|advanced|courses|choose-the-right)` → course_page
175	- `agilealliance.social`, `linkedin.com`, `facebook.com` → social_media
176	- `agilepainrelief.com/agile-checkup` or `scoreapp.com` → lead_magnet
177	- `agilepainrelief.com/where-is-ai` → webinar
178	- `agilepainrelief.com/$` or `/#` → homepage
179	- `Unsubscribe Link` / `View In Browser Link` → exclude
180	- Other external URLs → external_resource
181	
182	### 8. Newsletter-to-Website Traffic Correlation
183	
184	Connect newsletter link clicks to website traffic by matching clicked URLs to PostHog data filtered by `utm_source = drip`.
185	
186	### 9. Cross-Channel Content Performance
187	
188	For blog posts linked in newsletters AND shared on social, gather newsletter clicks + social engagement + PostHog pageviews by UTM source.
189	
190	## Workflow
191	
192	1. **Identify the question** — what is Mark asking about content performance?
193	2. **Load relevant data** from the Astro paths above
194	3. **Parse and correlate:**
195	   - Match social posts to traffic via links/pathnames
196	   - Match newsletter links via pathnames and `utm_source = drip`
197	   - Handle missing data gracefully (many posts lack engagement or traffic data; link detail only for recent newsletters)
198	4. **Present findings:**
199	   - Tables for comparisons
200	   - Highlight actionable insights
201	   - Note data limitations
202	5. **Save the report** to `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md` — overwrite, not date-stamp
203	
204	## Key Metrics
205	
206	| Metric | Source | What It Tells You |
207	|--------|--------|-------------------|
208	| LinkedIn impressions | history.json | Raw reach on LinkedIn |
209	| LinkedIn engagementRate | history.json | % of viewers who interacted |
210	| Mastodon favorites / reblogs | history.json | Resonance and shareability |
211	| Bluesky likes | history.json | Post resonance on Bluesky |
212	| Newsletter opens | newsletter-engagement.json | Email audience reach per issue |
213	| Newsletter CTR | newsletter-engagement.json | `clicks / opens * 100` — avg ~5.5%, top performers >10% |
214	| Newsletter unsub rate | newsletter-engagement.json | `unsubs / opens * 100` — avg ~0.66%, high >1% signals problems |
215	| Newsletter link clicks by category | newsletter-engagement.json | What link types readers actually click |
216	| Pageviews by UTM source | PostHog CSV | Social/email → website traffic |
217	| Session duration by source | PostHog CSV | Traffic quality by platform |
218	| Bounce rate by source/path | PostHog CSV | Content relevance to visitors |
219	
220	## Connecting Posts to Traffic
221	
222	1. A post in `history.json` has a `links` array (e.g. `["https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/some-post/"]`)
223	2. Buffer adds UTM parameters when posting (e.g. `?utm_source=mastodon`)
224	3. PostHog records the visit with the pathname and UTM source
225	4. Match on pathname to connect social post → website traffic
226	
227	Posts without links drive no direct measurable traffic.
228	
229	## Limitations
230	
231	### Social media
232	- Engagement data may be incomplete (not all posts scraped from Buffer)
233	- LinkedIn metrics are richer than Mastodon/Bluesky
234	- Topics array may be empty for older posts
235	
236	### Newsletter
237	- Per-link click detail only for ~13 newsletters from Aug 2025 onward
238	- Opens count is absolute, not rate of total subscribers (no recipient count available)
239	- Apple Mail Privacy Protection may inflate opens
240	- Pre-2022 newsletters have near-zero engagement (likely incomplete records)
241	
242	### Website
243	- PostHog CSVs are weekly snapshots, not continuous
244	- UTM tracking only works for links, not brand awareness / direct traffic
245	- Not all email clicks carry UTM parameters
246	
247	### Not in analytics at all
248	- **Number of students registered in courses** is not in the analytics folder
249	- **Revenue numbers** are not in the analytics folder
250	
251	Factor these gaps in when interpreting performance — social/newsletter engagement does not tell the full business story.
252	
253	## Example Prompts
254	
255	- "Which of my posts drove the most website traffic from Mastodon?"
256	- "How does traffic quality differ between LinkedIn and Mastodon?"
257	- "What topics get the most newsletter engagement?"
258	- "What links do newsletter readers actually click on?"
259	- "What content drives newsletter unsubscribes?"
260	- "How does blog post X perform across email and social?"
261	
262	For each, follow the method in the matching Analysis Type above and save the report to `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md`.
263	
264	---
265

- Google Search Console exports: `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro/analytics/google/`

**Analysis outputs (vault):**

- Single live report (overwrite, don't date): `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md`
- Newsletter findings reference: `APR/Analytics/email-engagement-findings.md`
- Newsletter content (for matching engagement to text): `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/*.md`
- Experiments tracking: `APR/Analytics/Experiments/`

**Writing one live report, not dated snapshots, is intentional** — Mark wants one place to look for current data. History is not important.

## Data Sources

### Post Engagement — `history.json`

Array of post objects. Each post has:

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `id` | number | Unique post identifier |
| `created` | string | Date post was created (YYYY-MM-DD) |
| `posted` | string | Date post was published (YYYY-MM-DD), empty if unposted |
| `linkedin` | string | LinkedIn post text |
| `mastodon` | array/string | Mastodon thread parts |
| `bluesky` | string | Bluesky thread text |
| `topics` | array | Topic tags (e.g. `["scrum", "agile"]`) |
| `links` | array | URLs included in the post |
| `engagement` | object | Per-platform engagement metrics (see below) |

#### Engagement metrics by platform

- **LinkedIn**: `reactions`, `comments`, `impressions`, `reach`, `engagementRate`
- **Mastodon**: `favorites`, `replies`, `reblogs`
- **Bluesky**: `likes`, `comments`, `reposts`

Not all posts have engagement on all platforms. Some posts have no engagement data at all.

### Email Newsletter Engagement — `newsletter-engagement.json`

Object with `lastUpdated` timestamp and `newsletters` array. Each newsletter has:

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `id` | string | Drip email identifier |
| `name` | string | Internal newsletter name |
| `subject` | string | Email subject line |
| `sendDate` | string | Date sent (YYYY-MM-DD), empty if unsent |
| `opens` | number | Email open count |
| `clicks` | number | Total link clicks |
| `unsubscribes` | number | Unsubscribe count from this email |
| `linkClicks` | array | Per-link click breakdown (recent newsletters only) |

Each item in `linkClicks` has: `url`, `text` (link label), `clicks` (count). Detail available from ~Aug 2025 onward.

#### Key metrics

- **Click-through rate (CTR)**: `clicks / opens * 100` — average is ~5.5%
- **Unsubscribe rate**: `unsubscribes / opens * 100` — average is ~0.66%
- **Link click categories**: blog_post, glossary_entry, course_page, external_resource, social_media, homepage, lead_magnet, webinar, lean_coffee, survey, waitlist_signup

#### Newsletter content source files

Full newsletter content (with all links, sections, and body text) is in Obsidian at `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/*.md`. Each file has YAML frontmatter with `id`, `subject`, `name`, `from_name`, `from_email`, `status`, `send_at`, and `created_at`. Match engagement records to content via the `id` field or by date/subject.

#### Established findings

Read `APR/Analytics/email-engagement-findings.md` for the durable findings:

- **Best-performing topic**: Meetings/facilitation (12.6% CTR, 0.18% unsub rate)
- **Strongest content format**: Long-form articles embedded in the email body
- **AI/GenAI topics**: Above-average CTR (6.57%), below-average unsub rate (0.59%)
- **Weakest performers**: Generic Scrum practice topics (3.18% CTR), abstract theory, pure announcements
- **Blog post clicks dominate**: 21.4% of all link clicks
- **Glossary entry clicks are minimal**: Only 1.3%
- **Mastodon profile link**: Surprisingly popular (167 clicks across 13 newsletters)
- **Opens declining**: 22% drop from 2023 peak to early 2026

### Website Traffic — PostHog CSVs

Three CSV files with date-stamped filenames (e.g. `*-2026-02-09.csv`). Use glob patterns to find the latest files.

#### Pageviews by week, UTM source, and pathname
- **File pattern**: `export-pageviews-by-week-utm-source-and-pathname-*.csv`
- **Columns**: `week`, `utm_source`, `pathname`, `daily_active_users`
- **UTM sources**: `mastodon`, `linkedin`, `drip` (email), `website`, `blog`, `chatgpt.com`, `None` (direct/organic)

#### Average session duration by UTM source by week
- **File pattern**: `export-average-sessions-by-utm-source-by-week-*.csv`
- **Columns**: `week`, `utm_source`, `total_sessions`, `avg_session_duration_seconds`, `avg_session_duration_minutes`

#### Bounce rate by UTM source and pathname
- **File pattern**: `export-bounce-rate-percentage-by-week-*.csv`
- **Columns**: `utm_source`, `pathname`, `bounced_sessions`, `total_sessions`, `bounce_rate_pct`

## Analysis Types

### 1. Cross-Platform Engagement Comparison

Compare how the same post performs across LinkedIn, Mastodon, and Bluesky.

**Method:** Read `history.json`, filter to posts with engagement on 2+ platforms, normalize metrics, identify platform-specific winners.

### 2. Social → Website Traffic Correlation

Connect social posts to website traffic by matching post links to PostHog pathnames.

**Method:** Read `history.json`, extract `links`, convert to pathnames. Read pageviews CSV, filter by `utm_source = mastodon` or `linkedin`. Match dates to weekly pageview data.

### 3. Topic Performance Analysis

Identify which topics generate the most engagement and traffic.

**Method:** Group `history.json` posts by `topics`, aggregate engagement across platforms, cross-reference PostHog pageviews for linked pages.

### 4. Traffic Source Quality

Compare how traffic from different social platforms behaves on the website.

**Method:** Compare session duration, bounce rate, and total visitors by UTM source across the three PostHog CSVs.

### 5. Content-to-Traffic Pipeline

End-to-end view: which posts drove the most qualified website traffic?

**Method:** Combine posts with links to agilepainrelief.com → PostHog traffic by path and UTM source → session duration → bounce rate. Rank by downstream website impact.

### 6. Posting Cadence Analysis

Group `history.json` posts by week/month using `posted` dates, calculate average engagement per period, compare high- vs. low-frequency weeks.

### 7. Newsletter Engagement Analysis

**Method:**
1. Filter `newsletter-engagement.json` to newsletters with opens > 100
2. Calculate CTR and unsub rate per newsletter
3. Categorize by topic from subject lines (AI/GenAI, Scrum Practices, Team/People, Meetings, Engineering/Quality, Metrics/Flow, Leadership, etc.)
4. Aggregate metrics per topic
5. For newsletters with `linkClicks` data, categorize each link and aggregate clicks by category

**Link categorization rules:**
- `agilepainrelief.com/blog/` → blog_post
- `agilepainrelief.com/glossary/` → glossary_entry
- `agilepainrelief.com/(certified|advanced|courses|choose-the-right)` → course_page
- `agilealliance.social`, `linkedin.com`, `facebook.com` → social_media
- `agilepainrelief.com/agile-checkup` or `scoreapp.com` → lead_magnet
- `agilepainrelief.com/where-is-ai` → webinar
- `agilepainrelief.com/$` or `/#` → homepage
- `Unsubscribe Link` / `View In Browser Link` → exclude
- Other external URLs → external_resource

### 8. Newsletter-to-Website Traffic Correlation

Connect newsletter link clicks to website traffic by matching clicked URLs to PostHog data filtered by `utm_source = drip`.

### 9. Cross-Channel Content Performance

For blog posts linked in newsletters AND shared on social, gather newsletter clicks + social engagement + PostHog pageviews by UTM source.

## Workflow

1. **Identify the question** — what is Mark asking about content performance?
2. **Load relevant data** from the Astro paths above
3. **Parse and correlate:**
   - Match social posts to traffic via links/pathnames
   - Match newsletter links via pathnames and `utm_source = drip`
   - Handle missing data gracefully (many posts lack engagement or traffic data; link detail only for recent newsletters)
4. **Present findings:**
   - Tables for comparisons
   - Highlight actionable insights
   - Note data limitations
5. **Save the report** to `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md` — overwrite, not date-stamp

## Key Metrics

| Metric | Source | What It Tells You |
|--------|--------|-------------------|
| LinkedIn impressions | history.json | Raw reach on LinkedIn |
| LinkedIn engagementRate | history.json | % of viewers who interacted |
| Mastodon favorites / reblogs | history.json | Resonance and shareability |
| Bluesky likes | history.json | Post resonance on Bluesky |
| Newsletter opens | newsletter-engagement.json | Email audience reach per issue |
| Newsletter CTR | newsletter-engagement.json | `clicks / opens * 100` — avg ~5.5%, top performers >10% |
| Newsletter unsub rate | newsletter-engagement.json | `unsubs / opens * 100` — avg ~0.66%, high >1% signals problems |
| Newsletter link clicks by category | newsletter-engagement.json | What link types readers actually click |
| Pageviews by UTM source | PostHog CSV | Social/email → website traffic |
| Session duration by source | PostHog CSV | Traffic quality by platform |
| Bounce rate by source/path | PostHog CSV | Content relevance to visitors |

## Connecting Posts to Traffic

1. A post in `history.json` has a `links` array (e.g. `["https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/some-post/"]`)
2. Buffer adds UTM parameters when posting (e.g. `?utm_source=mastodon`)
3. PostHog records the visit with the pathname and UTM source
4. Match on pathname to connect social post → website traffic

Posts without links drive no direct measurable traffic.

## Limitations

### Social media
- Engagement data may be incomplete (not all posts scraped from Buffer)
- LinkedIn metrics are richer than Mastodon/Bluesky
- Topics array may be empty for older posts

### Newsletter
- Per-link click detail only for ~13 newsletters from Aug 2025 onward
- Opens count is absolute, not rate of total subscribers (no recipient count available)
- Apple Mail Privacy Protection may inflate opens
- Pre-2022 newsletters have near-zero engagement (likely incomplete records)

### Website
- PostHog CSVs are weekly snapshots, not continuous
- UTM tracking only works for links, not brand awareness / direct traffic
- Not all email clicks carry UTM parameters

### Not in analytics at all
- **Number of students registered in courses** is not in the analytics folder
- **Revenue numbers** are not in the analytics folder

Factor these gaps in when interpreting performance — social/newsletter engagement does not tell the full business story.

## Example Prompts

- "Which of my posts drove the most website traffic from Mastodon?"
- "How does traffic quality differ between LinkedIn and Mastodon?"
- "What topics get the most newsletter engagement?"
- "What links do newsletter readers actually click on?"
- "What content drives newsletter unsubscribes?"
- "How does blog post X perform across email and social?"

For each, follow the method in the matching Analysis Type above and save the report to `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md`.

## Executive Summary

- **The direct-traffic bot spike has receded.** The latest complete week (07-20) fell to **1,562 total / 1,517 direct**, back to the ~1,400 human baseline after three inflated weeks (4,186 → 3,840 → 5,345). The anomaly appears over. Per Mark's standing call, direct stays untracked; noted here only because the numbers returned to normal.
- **A new newsletter went out July 21** ("Unintended AI Experiments — 150 Agents, 2 Useful Insights"): **3.91% CTR, 0.69% unsub** — a weak-to-middling send, the third soft send in a row. Clicks spread evenly across links (top link only 41), no concentration. Consistent with the pattern that experiment/roundup framing underconverts vs a concrete GenAI or facilitation hook.

1	
2	
3	The past couple of weeks have been full, between wildfire smoke and the elimination of England from the World Cup. I attended a Cycling Canada - cycling skill course (CAN-BIKE 4). I've been riding a bike for over 50 years. I assumed that I knew a lot. There was much to learn about how cars see (and don’t see) cyclists, how to participate in a group ride and survive Ottawa traffic. For once, I won't try to find a clever Agile analogy from this. GenAI gives me plenty to noodle on, so let's go there instead.
4	
5	If your current feelings on GenAI are, it's a steaming mess and should be buried, you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I'm going to touch on a few AI-related topics in this issue, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).
6	
7	## Canadian Government AI Strategy
8	Unlike many news outlets, I can’t do instant analysis and reflective thinking. I need time to noodle and digest. There is some good in the strategy: emphasis on safety and education. Sovereignty sounds like a good idea, until you realize that it just means building more data centres and investing in Canadian AI companies.
9	
10	The real problem is that the strategy defines the key pillar "Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity". When you dig into that pillar, we discover that they're measuring AI adoption as a proxy for prosperity/productivity. This is very funny. I'm sure we've all seen plenty of examples of AI adoption, where someone takes bullet points and asks ChatGPT to create a presentation. Faster than doing it manually? Yes. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person who created it learn anything meaningful about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.
11	
12	The strategy selects five areas to focus AI productivity on: Healthcare, Agriculture, Manufacturing, Energy and Natural Resources, and Transportation. I know a bit about healthcare and so I focused on it, in [Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/).
13	
14	Instead of dealing with the hard work of making systemic improvements to the healthcare (or other) system, the strategy is betting on a magic wand.
15	
16	I'm also thinking that we will see a lot of "AI Washing" in the next few years. I think existing machine learning will be rebranded as AI.
17	
18	## From AI Washing to Bigger isn’t always Better
19	In booster circles, I hear two suggestions: next week's model (Fable) will solve all the existing problems and use agents to offset other agents mistakes (Opus).
20	
21	I've had two experiences in the past few weeks that highlight the problem with both suggestions. I used Claude Fable to do a security audit of the Personal Expense Tracker App I’m building. I accidentally used agents with Claude Opus when I wanted to understand what lead magnets currently work to get people to sign up for a newsletter.
22	
23	### Fable Security Audit
24	Anthropic has limited access to the Fable model, which they previously touted for its ability to do security audits. Since I'm building an application and I'm not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to have Fable do an audit. Based on reviewing other people’s experience with Fable, its strength is chaining together multiple steps into a single exploit. Sure enough, it found one key vulnerability and a bunch of minor ones. What I didn’t expect: it used up my entire daily usage limit, and I had to wait for it to reset that evening. The best part? My security flaw was the result of a hastily implemented bug fix from earlier in the week. 
25	
26	The frontier labs don't generally talk about how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi K3 was just released and it claims to be in the same league as Claude Opus 4.8[^kimi-opus]. The Kimi K3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters[^kimi-params]. Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better through massive amounts of RAM and compute. So: progress by throwing more of everything at the problem.
27	
28	### Opus Research Task
29	I asked Opus to do some research on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for "deep research" - don't do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would do a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further, it decided that it would use a 3-vote rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. Then the individual agents were asked to vote on the claim they were analysing. The result was that 50 claims were evaluated by 150 agents. It took 30 minutes to burn through my usage limit and I had to wait for it to reset that evening to finish the task.
30	
31	For that much compute, I was expecting a nice long report with real depth. Instead, I got a 3-page report with two good insights.
32	
33	Agents are not necessarily better. I may well need a much longer blog post to explain why. The short version: assume each agent is imperfect at the task. You can't mask the imperfections of one agent with another. If anything, I would expect the imperfections to multiply.
34	
35	## Big Ask
36	One of the two insights from Opus's Research Task? Ask your newsletter readers for referrals. To quote Opus: "single most effective newsletter growth strategy is **direct recommendations from existing subscribers (word-of-mouth/referral)**". I'm supposed to offer you a discount or a free trial in return. In practice, I can't see what I would offer at the moment.

The past couple of weeks have been full, between wildfire smoke and the elimination of England from the World Cup. I attended a Cycling Canada - cycling skill course (CAN-BIKE 4). I've been riding a bike for over 50 years. I assumed that I knew a lot. There was much to learn about how cars see (and don’t see) cyclists, how to participate in a group ride and survive Ottawa traffic. For once, I won't try to find a clever Agile analogy from this. GenAI gives me plenty to noodle on, so let's go there instead.

If your current feelings on GenAI are, it's a steaming mess and should be buried, you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I'm going to touch on a few AI-related topics in this issue, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).

## Canadian Government AI Strategy
Unlike many news outlets, I can’t do instant analysis and reflective thinking. I need time to noodle and digest. There is some good in the strategy: emphasis on safety and education. Sovereignty sounds like a good idea, until you realize that it just means building more data centres and investing in Canadian AI companies.

The real problem is that the strategy defines the key pillar "Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity". When you dig into that pillar, we discover that they're measuring AI adoption as a proxy for prosperity/productivity. This is very funny. I'm sure we've all seen plenty of examples of AI adoption, where someone takes bullet points and asks ChatGPT to create a presentation. Faster than doing it manually? Yes. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person who created it learn anything meaningful about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.

The strategy selects five areas to focus AI productivity on: Healthcare, Agriculture, Manufacturing, Energy and Natural Resources, and Transportation. I know a bit about healthcare and so I focused on it, in [Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/).

Instead of dealing with the hard work of making systemic improvements to the healthcare (or other) system, the strategy is betting on a magic wand.

I'm also thinking that we will see a lot of "AI Washing" in the next few years. I think existing machine learning will be rebranded as AI.

## From AI Washing to Bigger isn’t always Better
In booster circles, I hear two suggestions: next week's model (Fable) will solve all the existing problems and use agents to offset other agents mistakes (Opus).

I've had two experiences in the past few weeks that highlight the problem with both suggestions. I used Claude Fable to do a security audit of the Personal Expense Tracker App I’m building. I accidentally used agents with Claude Opus when I wanted to understand what lead magnets currently work to get people to sign up for a newsletter.

### Fable Security Audit
Anthropic has limited access to the Fable model, which they previously touted for its ability to do security audits. Since I'm building an application and I'm not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to have Fable do an audit. Based on reviewing other people’s experience with Fable, its strength is chaining together multiple steps into a single exploit. Sure enough, it found one key vulnerability and a bunch of minor ones. What I didn’t expect: it used up my entire daily usage limit, and I had to wait for it to reset that evening. The best part? My security flaw was the result of a hastily implemented bug fix from earlier in the week. 

The frontier labs don't generally talk about how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi K3 was just released and it claims to be in the same league as Claude Opus 4.8[^kimi-opus]. The Kimi K3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters[^kimi-params]. Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better through massive amounts of RAM and compute. So: progress by throwing more of everything at the problem.

### Opus Research Task
I asked Opus to do some research on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for "deep research" - don't do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would do a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further, it decided that it would use a 3-vote rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. Then the individual agents were asked to vote on the claim they were analysing. The result was that 50 claims were evaluated by 150 agents. It took 30 minutes to burn through my usage limit and I had to wait for it to reset that evening to finish the task.

For that much compute, I was expecting a nice long report with real depth. Instead, I got a 3-page report with two good insights.

Agents are not necessarily better. I may well need a much longer blog post to explain why. The short version: assume each agent is imperfect at the task. You can't mask the imperfections of one agent with another. If anything, I would expect the imperfections to multiply.

## Big Ask
One of the two insights from Opus's Research Task? Ask your newsletter readers for referrals. To quote Opus: "single most effective newsletter growth strategy is **direct recommendations from existing subscribers (word-of-mouth/referral)**". I'm supposed to offer you a discount or a free trial in return. In practice, I can't see what I would offer at the moment.

If you get value from this newsletter, please share it with a friend. If someone shared it with you, click here to subscribe.
