Got it, and my wording was loose. Let me clear all three up.

## 1. The July 21 "experiment" (my label was misleading)

It wasn't a *marketing* experiment in the tracked sense. I was describing the **newsletter's own theme**. The July 21 issue was titled "Unintended AI Experiments — 150 Agents, 2 Useful Insights," and it was built around two accidents you had with AI tools:

- **The Fable security audit** of your Expense Tracker app (found one real vuln, but burned your whole daily limit).
- **The Opus "deep research" task** on lead magnets, where Opus spun up **150 agents** (50 claims × 3 voting agents each), ran 30 minutes, blew through your usage cap, and returned a thin 3-page report with only two useful insights.

Plus the Canada AI-strategy piece and AI-washing musings. So "150 Agents, 2 Useful Insights" = that Opus story.

My point in the report was about **structure, not topic**: it read as a loose roundup of four AI musings rather than one focused hook. Your CTR winners have all been single, concrete, promise-what-you-deliver pieces. Two diffuse-structure sends in a row (July 8 WIP, July 21 roundup) both landed under 4%. The AI content is fine; the scattered format is what I suspect underconverts.

## 2. A GenAI facilitation hook for the next newsletter

"Facilitation" is your single best-performing newsletter topic historically (meetings/facilitation ~12.6% CTR). GenAI is your other above-average pillar. A "GenAI facilitation hook" just **fuses the two**: a concrete piece about where AI actually touches the work of running teams and meetings. A few angles, most concrete first:

- **"I let AI take my retro notes for a month. Here's what it missed."** A specific first-person test: what GenAI captured well in a retrospective vs the human signal (tension, hesitation, the unspoken) it flattened. Ties straight to your deskilling thread.
- **"Should the ScrumMaster use ChatGPT to write the working agreement?"** A single sharp question, answered with a real example. Your July 22 working-agreement post already touched this on Mastodon.
- **"AI can summarize your Daily Scrum. That's exactly the problem."** Argues the value of the meeting is the conversation, not the summary; automating the artifact misses the point. Pairs with your "making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity" line from July 21.

The common thread: one question, one story, one promise in the subject line, delivered in the body. That's the shape that converts for you, not a roundup.

## 3. The deskilling blog/newsletter treatment

This is a traffic observation, not a content idea I invented. The glossary stub **`/glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/`** has held ~370-380 pageviews for two-plus weeks now, *weeks after* the July 15 "Deskilling" social posts that first drove it. That kind of durable, self-sustaining traffic on a thin glossary page is a signal that the topic has legs.

The suggestion: **turn that demand into a fuller asset.** Options, lightest first:

- **Expand the glossary entry itself** into a proper explainer (what deskilling is, the academic evidence you referenced July 15, why it matters for teams using GenAI). Low effort, feeds an already-ranking page.
- **A full blog post** on GenAI deskilling in knowledge work, with the glossary entry linking up to it as the pillar. This also feeds your GenAI content-cluster strategy (the internal-linking experiment).
- **A newsletter issue** on the theme, which would double as one of the concrete-hook sends from point 2 above ("Losing the skills you stop using has a name").

The three connect: a deskilling newsletter *is* a concrete GenAI hook, and it could point at an expanded blog/glossary page. One theme, three surfaces.

Want me to draft any of these, or capture them to OmniFocus?

---
title: 'AI and Skill Atrophy - Anti-Pattern'
date: '2026-02-24'
lastUpdated: '2026-02-24'
relatedTerms:
  - 'anti-patterns'
  - 'cross-skilling'
  - 'systems-thinking'
  - 'feature-factory'
excerpt: "Software's knowledge cliff: GenAI reliance erodes skills we don't practice. Juniors hit hardest with false confidence. Radiology detection fails without AI; NASA docs but no understanding."
---

import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
import DeskillingCLD from '@/content/glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/images/deskilling-cld.png';

We're losing skills because we don't use them, and we're not growing the developers of the future. What do we give up to LLMs?

When you use an LLM to make a decision you could make without the LLM, you gain a sense of false confidence. The easier it is to prompt an LLM to produce an answer, the less we develop the skill. This affects junior people more than senior people, since they have less overall experience to base their skills on.

In the academic literature, this is called Deskilling. In radiology, AI assistants help detect abnormalities in medical images. In theory, these detect problems faster and don’t get tired. (In practice, there are open questions about their effectiveness.) Too much reliance on AI leaves the radiologist unable to detect on their own. Bad enough for the senior radiologists, but even worse for new doctors. When the AI Assistant was used in the learning process, the new doctor didn't have as deep an understanding of what they were seeing.

This is a knowledge cliff, and the software industry is headed to one. (Hat tip to Brian Graham for the term.)

NASA has been through this recently; they want to build big rockets again. They have mountains of documentation (literally 2900 cubic feet), but they don't have the understanding and tacit knowledge to use it.

## Effects of Deskilling
- **Team Impact**: Reduced mentorship and knowledge sharing.
- **Long-Term Risk**: Novel or unexpected problems can't easily be solved with AI, leaving people unprepared.
- **Cognitive Atrophy**: Over-reliance on GenAI increases confidence in the AI while diminishing critical thinking skills.

<Figure
  src={DeskillingCLD}
  alt="Causal loop diagram showing how LLM Reliance reduces Skill Practice, which reduces Developer Skill and Tacit Knowledge, ultimately diminishing the Ability to Solve Novel Problems, which in turn increases LLM Reliance"
  caption="Deskilling Causal Loop Diagram"
/>

Brian Graham offers a question list: before automating with AI, ask:
- **Knowledge assessment** - do we understand the domain well enough to evaluate the AI output?
- Is this a **Core competency** vs **Background noise**?
- **Failure Planning** - Are we monitoring and prepared to reverse course if this decision fails?

The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.

Pilots have been through this before. With the advent of autopilot, instrument landing systems, automated flight management systems, etc., these systems have reduced the need for certain piloting skills. To combat this, they have increased the amount of training and simulator time for pilots to maintain their certifications.

*I did not mention the 2026 Anthropic study: "How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills", because there are enough questions about the design and methodology that I don’t see it as a reliable source.*

Deskilling and knowledge cliffs are a full module of our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/), an evidence-based, cohort-based course for Agile teams.

We unpack how AI adoption can weaken personal autonomy, reduces motivation, and strains relationships' 10 --- 11 import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro'; 12 import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro'; 13 import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro'; 14 import humanCostGenai from '@/content/blog/the-human-cost-of-genai/images/the-human-cost-of-genai.jpg' 15 16 Generative AI is helping people be more productive (sometimes). Of course, if you're worried about [defects or accuracy](/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/), it's [not all that it's cracked up to be](/blog/the-real-cost-of-ai-generated-code-it-s-not-all-it-s-cracked-up-to-be/) but, sure, for things like reviewing writing for grammatical errors, prototyping features and applications, and gathering data when accuracy isn't essential, it's helpful. It also speeds discovery and brainstorming (sometimes[^1]). 17 18 So, yes, it's (sometimes) helping people be more productive and there are (some) places where it does make (some) things get done faster. 19 20 But forget about speed for a minute, which is what all the focus seems to be on, and let's put some thought into the consequences of all this so-called productivity. **The human cost.** (One specific cost: [AI and Skill Atrophy](/glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/), where the very skills we stop practising start to fade.) 21 22 (*_Caveat: the research in this area is new and will evolve._) 23 24 The human cost of GenAI is a full module in our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/), an evidence-based, cohort-based course for Agile teams. 25 26 ## Productive But Less Motivated 27 From the Harvard Business Review: "Research: Gen AI Makes People More Productive—and Less Motivated"[^2] and [^3] 28 29 In this study, people who used GenAI for tasks like writing emails, social media posts, and brainstorming were more productive. But this productivity came at a cost. 30 31 As GenAI takes over the demanding tasks, people report lower intrinsic motivation and increased boredom. This leads to disengagement and dissatisfaction with work and, if unchecked, burnout. 32 33 Using the ARC Motivational model, we know that we need to feel competence in doing our work. The use of GenAI is taking away from that sense of effectiveness and confidence, leaving people to ask: Why am I here? 34 35 ## Loss of Control and Connection 36 > Employees who excel with AI tools are **twice** as likely to consider leaving their organizations, pointing directly to the pressure of their overwhelming workload. 37 38 Upwork Research Institute surveyed over three thousand people to understand how GenAI is affecting people at work.[^4] Since it is a survey, this is self-reported information and not a rigorously designed experiment, so we need to be careful about the strength of the conclusions we draw. 39 40 > Adam described his company's owner as someone who "thinks every new AI function will propel us to the next level with minimal effort," a mindset with which he strongly disagrees. 41 > … the challenge wasn't resistance to AI but rather overenthusiasm without a grounded understanding of what AI can and can't do. 42 43 Many organizations are mandating the use of GenAI to increase productivity, without considering the broader consequences. When poorly implemented, these mandates lead to the feeling that we have no control or agency in the work. Even when the use of AI isn't imposed, people report that they feel less in control if the tool is doing many of the tasks for them. 44 45 Autonomy is central to both the ARC and SCARF motivational models. As humans, we need to feel that we have choices and agency. The use of GenAI is reducing that for many workers. 46

Read by other Readwise skills that hit the CLI." 7 dependencies: ["None (read at runtime by other Readwise skills)"] 8 description: How to use the Readwise CLI — access highlights, documents, and your entire reading library from the command line 9 --- 10 11 # Readwise CLI 12 13 Use the `readwise` command to access the user's Readwise highlights and Reader documents. Readwise has two products: 14 15 - **Readwise** — highlights from books, articles, podcasts, and more. Includes daily review and spaced repetition. 16 - **Reader** — a read-later app for saving and reading articles, PDFs, EPUBs, RSS feeds, emails, tweets, and videos. 17 18 ## Setup 19 20 If `readwise` is not installed: 21 ```bash 22 npm install -g @readwise/cli 23 ``` 24 25 If not authenticated, ask the user for their Readwise access token (they can get one at https://readwise.io/access_token), then run: 26 ```bash 27 readwise login-with-token 28 ``` 29 30 ## Discovering Commands 31 32 Every command supports `--help` for full option details: 33 ```bash 34 readwise --help 35 readwise reader-search-documents --help 36 readwise readwise-list-highlights --help 37 ``` 38 39 Add `--json` to any command for machine-readable output. Use `--refresh` to force-refresh cached data. 40 41 ## Reader Commands 42 43 ### Searching documents 44 45 ```bash 46 # Semantic search across all saved documents 47 readwise reader-search-documents --query "spaced repetition" 48 49 # Search only articles saved for later 50 readwise reader-search-documents --query "machine learning" --category-in article --location-in later,shortlist 51 52 # Search by author within the inbox 53 readwise reader-search-documents --query "AI" --author-search "Simon Willison" --location-in new 54 55 # Search documents published after a date 56 readwise reader-search-documents --query "transformers" --published-date-gt 2024-01-01 57 ``` 58 59 ### Browsing documents 60 61 ```bash 62 # List 10 most recent inbox items (minimal fields to save tokens) 63 readwise reader-list-documents --location new --limit 10 --response-fields title,author,summary,word_count,category,saved_at 64 65 # List archived articles tagged "research" 66 readwise reader-list-documents --location archive --tag research --category article 67 68 # List unseen documents in the inbox 69 readwise reader-list-documents --location new --seen false 70 71 # List RSS feed items 72 readwise reader-list-documents --location feed --limit 20 --response-fields title,author,summary,site_name 73 74 # Get a specific document by ID 75 readwise reader-list-documents --id 76 ``` 77 78 Locations: `new` (inbox), `later`, `shortlist`, `archive`, `feed`. When the user says "inbox", use `new`. 79 80 ### Reading and highlighting 81 82 ```bash 83 # Get full document content as Markdown 84 readwise reader-get-document-details --document-id 85 86 # Get all highlights on a document 87 readwise reader-get-document-highlights --document-id 88 89 # Highlight a passage (html-content must match the document's HTML exactly) 90 # Get the HTML first via reader-list-documents with --response-fields html_content 91 readwise reader-create-highlight --document-id --html-content "

The exact passage to highlight

" 92 93 # Highlight with a note and tags 94 readwise reader-create-highlight --document-id --html-content "

Key insight

" --note "Connects to spaced repetition research" --tags review,concept 95 ``` 96 97 ### Saving documents 98 99 ```bash 100 # Save a URL — Reader scrapes it automatically 101 readwise reader-create-document --url "https://example.com/article" 102 103 # Save with metadata 104 readwise reader-create-document --url "https://example.com" --title "Great Article" --tags research,ai --notes "Recommended by Alice" 105 106 # Save raw Markdown content (provide a unique URL as identifier) 107 readwise reader-create-document --title "Meeting Notes" --markdown "# Notes from today..." --url "https://me.com#notes-march-2025" 108 ``` 109 110 ### Organizing 111 112 ```bash 113 # Move documents between locations (max 50 per call) 114 readwise reader-move-documents --document-ids , --location archive 115 readwise reader-move-documents --document-ids --location later 116 117 # Bulk mark documents as seen 118 readwise reader-bulk-edit-document-metadata --documents '[{"document_id": "", "seen": true}]' 119 120 # Bulk update metadata (title, author, tags, summary, etc.) 121 readwise reader-bulk-edit-document-metadata --documents '[{"document_id": "", "title": "Better Title", "tags": ["ai", "research"]}]' 122 123 # Tags 124 readwise reader-list-tags 125 readwise reader-add-tags-to-document --document-id --tag-names important,research 126 readwise reader-remove-tags-from-document --document-id --tag-names old-tag 127 128 # Highlight tags and notes 129 readwise reader-add-tags-to-highlight --document-id --highlight-document-id --tag-names concept 130 readwise reader-remove-tags-from-highlight --document-id --highlight-document-id --tag-names old-tag 131 readwise reader-set-highlight-notes --document-id --highlight-document-id --notes "Updated note" 132 ``` 133 134 ### Exporting 135 136 ```bash 137 # Export all documents as a ZIP of Markdown files (async) 138 readwise reader-export-documents 139 readwise reader-get-export-documents-status --export-id 140 141 # Delta export — only docs updated since last export 142 readwise reader-export-documents --since-updated "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z" 143 ``` 144 145 ## Readwise Commands 146 147 ### Searching highlights 148 149 ```bash 150 # Semantic search across all highlights 151 readwise readwise-search-highlights --vector-search-term "learning techniques" 152 153 # Search with full-text filter on a specific field 154 readwise readwise-search-highlights --vector-search-term "memory" --full-text-queries '[{"field_name": "document_title", "search_term": "psychology"}]' 155 ``` 156 157 Full-text query fields: `document_author`, `document_title`, `highlight_note`, `highlight_plaintext`, `highlight_tags`. 158 159 ### Browsing highlights 160 161 ```bash 162 # List 20 most recent highlights 163 readwise readwise-list-highlights --page-size 20 164 165 # Highlights from a specific book 166 readwise readwise-list-highlights --book-id 167 168 # Highlights from the last month 169 readwise readwise-list-highlights --highlighted-at-gt "2025-02-01T00:00:00Z" 170 ``` 171 172 ### Creating and editing highlights 173 174 ```bash 175 # Create a highlight (matched to a book by title/author, or goes into "Quotes") 176 readwise readwise-create-highlights --highlights '[{"text": "The key insight here", "title": "Book Title", "author": "Author Name"}]' 177 178 # Create multiple highlights at once 179 readwise readwise-create-highlights --highlights '[{"text": "First quote", "title": "Book A"}, {"text": "Second quote", "title": "Book B"}]' 180 181 # Update a highlight — text, note, color, tags 182 readwise readwise-update-highlight --highlight-id --note "New note" --add-tags concept,review --color blue 183 184 # Delete a highlight 185 readwise readwise-delete-highlight --highlight-id 186 ``` 187 188 Colors: `yellow`, `blue`, `pink`, `orange`, `green`, `purple`. 189 190 ### Daily review 191 192 ```bash 193 # Get today's spaced repetition review 194 readwise readwise-get-daily-review 195 ``` 196 197 Returns highlights selected by the spaced repetition algorithm plus a URL for interactive review. 198 199 ## Example Workflows 200 201 **Triage the inbox:** List recent saves, read each one, decide what's worth the user's time. 202 ```bash 203 readwise reader-list-documents --location new --limit 10 --response-fields title,author,summary,word_count,category,saved_at 204 readwise reader-get-document-details --document-id 205 readwise reader-move-documents --document-ids --location later # worth reading 206 readwise reader-move-documents --document-ids --location archive # skip 207 ``` 208 209 **Search across everything:** Find all content on a topic across both highlights and documents. 210 ```bash 211 readwise reader-search-documents --query "spaced repetition" 212 readwise readwise-search-highlights --vector-search-term "spaced repetition" 213 ``` 214 215 **Quiz on a recent read:** Find a finished document, get its content and highlights, quiz the user. 216 ```bash 217 readwise reader-list-documents --location archive --limit 10 --response-fields title,author,summary,word_count 218 readwise reader-get-document-details --document-id 219 readwise reader-get-document-highlights --document-id 220 ``` 221 222 **Catch up on RSS:** Browse feed items, surface the best ones, mark the rest as seen. 223 ```bash 224 readwise reader-list-documents --location feed --limit 20 --response-fields title,author,summary,word_count,site_name 225 readwise reader-bulk-edit-document-metadata --documents '[{"document_id": "", "seen": true}]' 226 readwise reader-move-documents --document-ids --location later 227 ``` 228 229 **Save and annotate:** Save a URL, highlight key passages, tag and organize. 230 ```bash 231 readwise reader-create-document --url "https://example.com/article" --tags research 232 readwise reader-create-highlight --document-id --html-content "

Key passage here

" --note "This connects to..." 233 readwise reader-add-tags-to-document --document-id --tag-names important 234 ``` 235 236 **Build a reading recap:** See what you've finished and highlighted recently. 237 ```bash 238 readwise reader-list-documents --location archive --updated-after "2025-03-10T00:00:00Z" --response-fields title,author,word_count,reading_progress 239 readwise reader-get-document-highlights --document-id 240 readwise readwise-list-highlights --highlighted-at-gt "2025-03-10T00:00:00Z" --page-size 50 241 ``` 242

All 8 moved to your Reader shortlist. Here's the angle thinking and the list.

## What angle is different enough?

Your existing coverage already owns two territories:

- **The glossary** owns the *mechanism and definition*: false confidence, juniors hit hardest, radiology/NASA/pilots examples, Brian Graham's knowledge cliff and question list, the causal loop diagram.
- **The Human Cost of GenAI** owns the *wellbeing angle*: motivation, autonomy, connection, burnout, team cohesion (ARC/SCARF).

So a new post shouldn't re-explain what deskilling is or why it hurts morale. Three angles that are genuinely open:

**A. "Where do the next senior engineers come from?" (recommended)**
The pipeline/succession angle. Juniors who let AI skip the struggle never build the judgment that struggle forges, so in five years there's no senior tier to review the AI's work. Your glossary has a single undeveloped line about "not growing the developers of the future" - this is the post that develops it. It's a *leadership and org-design* argument, which fits your ScrumMaster/coach audience and is distinct from both existing pieces. Forward-looking, and it's the point you gestured at in the July 21 newsletter.

**B. The reviewer's dilemma: you can't review what you can't write.**
As we deskill, the very skill that lets us catch AI's mistakes erodes, and that's a reinforcing loop. This one plugs straight into your strongest-trafficked pillar (GenAI code quality), so it's the most strategically connected. Strong as either its own post or the backbone of A.

**C. Keeping skills sharp: a team practice playbook (ScrumMaster lens).**
The glossary is diagnostic; this would be prescriptive. Deliberate AI-free reps, pairing/ensemble, rotation, "simulator time" like pilots. Pairs with your Effective Scrum framing.

My lean: **A as the spine, borrowing B's reviewer-loop as the sharpest supporting argument.** That gives you a leadership-audience post that doesn't overlap the glossary or Human Cost, and it lets the newsletter version carry the concrete hook ("In five years, who reviews the AI?").
